title: Emergency Deviation Approval Chain During AS9100 Audit
scenario: You're preparing for an AS9100D surveillance audit next week. The auditor has requested complete traceability for Lot #J4782 (titanium valve bodies for aerospace customer Northstar Aero, shipped April 2026). In SAP QM, you find the lot was released with a Material Review Board (MRB) disposition: 'Use As Is' approved by Quality Manager Sarah Chen on April 18, 2026 at 14:32. The NCR (NCR-2026-0447) references a dimensional deviation on bore diameter (spec: 12.50mm ±0.02mm, actual: 12.53mm). The SAP record shows Sarah's digital signature and references ECN-5429 as 'pending engineering review.' In MasterControl, ECN-5429 shows status 'Draft' with no approvals - it was initiated April 19 (day after the MRB) by Design Engineer Mike Torres but never routed for signature. However, in the ECN comments field, there's a note from May 3: 'Per Mike's exit interview checklist, transferring ownership to J. Park.' You check Jira and find Mike Torres's last day was April 30, 2026. In a Microsoft Teams chat dated April 17 at 16:45 (day before the MRB decision), Plant Manager Bob Kowalski messaged Sarah: 'Talked to Dave at Northstar - they're OK with the bore being slightly over, needs to clear their tolerance stack. Dave will send email blessing tomorrow but we need to ship tonight for their production line. Can you push the MRB through? I'll take the heat if audit finds it.' You find no email from Northstar's Dave in the shared quality inbox. The PPAP documentation for this part (Rev C, approved 2024) shows the original design authority was Chief Engineer Linda Voss, who retired in December 2025. Current delegation matrix in SharePoint (updated March 2026) shows her authorities transferred to Engineering Director James Palmer for all active aerospace programs.
question: Who had the authority to approve the 'Use As Is' disposition for Lot #J4782 under your AS9100D procedures?
choices: A) Bob Kowalski (Plant Manager) - he secured customer concession from Northstar prior to the MRB
B) No one - the disposition was invalid because ECN-5429 was never completed and the original design authority (Linda Voss) had retired
C) Sarah Chen (Quality Manager) - her digital signature in SAP QM constitutes valid MRB approval
D) James Palmer (Engineering Director) - as the delegated design authority, only he could authorize deviation from drawing specification
rationale: Under AS9100D clause 8.5.1.2, deviations from design specifications require authorization from the design authority (or delegate) and customer concession where contractually required. The critical signal is buried in the SharePoint delegation matrix: Linda Voss's design authority transferred to James Palmer in March 2026. Palmer's approval is absent from all records, making the lot release non-compliant. Answer A fails because Bob Kowalski's Teams message claims customer approval, but (1) there's no documented evidence — the promised email from Northstar's Dave never arrived, and (2) a Plant Manager cannot substitute for the design authority regardless of customer sentiment. Answer B fails because the disposition is not inherently invalid — a proper approval path existed through James Palmer as delegated design authority. The ECN-5429 never being completed is irrelevant to MRB authority (ECNs document changes, not dispositions), and Linda Voss's retirement doesn't create a void because her authority was formally transferred. Answer C fails because Sarah Chen's Quality Manager role allows her to document MRB proceedings and sign the disposition record, but she cannot independently authorize deviation from engineering drawing specifications — that requires the design authority per AS9100D. The audit finding would be: proper design authority (Palmer) was never consulted, revealing a systemic gap between documented procedures and the actual ship-first-document-later practice exposed in the Teams chat.

title: CAPA Procedure Revision During Multi-Month Investigation
scenario: CAPA-2026-0089 was initiated February 12, 2026 for recurring weld porosity failures in automotive transmission housings (customer: Midwest Automotive Systems). Root cause investigation spanned four months due to complexity. The CAPA record in MasterControl shows: Initiated 2/12/26, Root Cause Analysis completed 5/8/26, Corrective Action Plan approved 5/22/26, Implementation target 6/15/26. During your monthly management review meeting on June 25, the Quality Director notes that CAPA-2026-0089 is overdue for closure and asks why effectiveness verification wasn't completed within the 90-day target. You review the case timeline. Your CAPA procedure QP-08-002 was at Rev F when this CAPA initiated (effective date: January 15, 2026). That revision required: Root cause within 30 days, corrective action plan within 60 days, implementation within 90 days, effectiveness check at 30 days post-implementation. However, you notice in the SharePoint quality manual folder that QP-08-002 Rev G was published April 1, 2026 (effective date: April 15, 2026) with revised timelines: Root cause within 45 days, corrective action plan within 90 days, implementation within 120 days for 'complex manufacturing process CAPAs' (new category), effectiveness check at 60 days post-implementation. In a Teams channel message dated April 28, Quality Engineer Amy Liu posted: 'Heads up - talked to Henrik, he confirmed CAPA-0089 qualifies as complex manufacturing under new Rev G. Updating my tracker accordingly.' You have no memory of this conversation, but Amy left the company in May (exit date: 5/17/26) and her successor Mark Chen is now managing CAPA-0089. The MasterControl CAPA record header still references 'Procedure: QP-08-002 Rev F' and hasn't been updated. The corrective action (installation of automated weld parameter monitoring system) was completed June 10, 2026, and the first verification samples are scheduled for July 15 (35 days post-implementation, splitting the difference between Rev F's 30 days and Rev G's 60 days).
question: Under which procedure revision should CAPA-2026-0089 be evaluated for timeline compliance?
choices: A) Rev F - the revision in effect when the CAPA was initiated governs the entire lifecycle
B) Rev G - it became effective April 15, before the Root Cause Analysis was completed, and applies to all open CAPAs
C) Rev F for phases completed before April 15; Rev G for phases completed after April 15 (hybrid application)
D) Rev G - Amy Liu's Teams message and Henrik's verbal confirmation constitute documented reclassification to 'complex manufacturing'
rationale: The fundamental principle in quality management system procedures is that the revision in effect at case initiation governs the entire case lifecycle unless there is a formal documented transition process. CAPA-2026-0089 was initiated February 12 under QP-08-002 Rev F, and that revision's requirements bind the case through closure. Choice B fails because procedure revisions don't automatically apply retroactively to open cases - this would create compliance chaos as targets shift mid-investigation. Choice C (hybrid application) is administratively untenable and creates ambiguity about which standard applies to overall case evaluation. Choice D is the most tempting wrong answer: Amy's Teams message claiming Henrik's verbal approval seems to document a reclassification to 'complex manufacturing' under Rev G. However, this is an informal channel communication with no formal documentation trail. Amy's departure means the claimed conversation cannot be verified, and the MasterControl header still references Rev F. The critical gap: there's no formal change control record showing the CAPA was officially transitioned to Rev G governance. The Teams message represents the actual practice (informal flexibility), but during an audit or management review, the documented procedure version at initiation controls. The Quality Director's concern about 90-day target (Rev F) is technically valid, though the investigation legitimately needed more time. Proper practice would have been: either (1) extend timeline via formal CAPA extension request under Rev F, or (2) formally document transition to Rev G with change justification in MasterControl.

title: Traceability Gap in Material Revision Changeover
scenario: Your customer Precision Aerospace has issued a field service bulletin requiring identification of all parts shipped between March 15 and April 30, 2026 for potential recall. The affected component is part number 7840-A-REV3 (aluminum mounting bracket). In SAP, you query production history and find 847 units shipped during the window across 8 lot numbers. The drawing revision history in your PLM system shows: Rev 2 (effective through March 22, 2026, 10:00 AM), Rev 3 (effective March 22, 2026, 10:00 AM onwards). ECN-5381 documents the Rev 2→3 change: material specification changed from Alloy 6061-T6 to 6063-T6 for cost reduction. The ECN was approved March 15 and released for production March 22. Your SAP material master shows part number 7840-A-REV3 was created March 22 at 09:15 (before the 10:00 AM effectivity time - IT created the record in advance). You examine the 8 lot numbers: Lots J4801-J4805 (produced March 18-21) show material code MAT-6061T6-LD (legacy material code from the 2018 ERP migration). Lots J4811-J4813 (produced March 25-April 28) show material code AL-6063-T6-STD (the current code format from 2024). However, in the Cleveland plant's maintenance Excel tracker (\\shared\Plant1\maintenance-log.xlsx), you find an entry dated March 23, 08:30 AM: 'Forklift damaged 4 pallets of 6063 alloy in receiving. Material quarantined. Borrowed 2 pallets of 6061 from WIP inventory (old stock, Lot J4799) to keep Line 3 running. Shift supervisor Tony approved. Will replenish when new 6063 delivery arrives 3/25.' This entry was made by Jerry Santos, a maintenance tech who doesn't enter data in SAP. You cross-reference: Lot J4811 (first lot showing 6063 in SAP) was produced March 23, 11:00 AM - 7:45 PM. The forklift incident occurred at 8:30 AM that same day. Production records in SAP show Line 3 ran continuously March 23, no downtime. The 'borrowed' 6061 material from Lot J4799 (produced February 2026 under Rev 2) isn't traced in SAP because it was an informal plant-floor material substitution. First Article Inspection (FAI) for Rev 3 was completed March 24 using Lot J4812 material (definitively 6063 alloy).
question: Which lots require inclusion in the potential recall investigation for material specification discrepancy?
choices: A) Lots J4801-J4805 only - they were produced before the Rev 3 effectivity date and may have been mislabeled
B) All 8 lots (J4801-J4813) - the SAP material master was created before effectivity time, creating traceability uncertainty
C) Lots J4801-J4805 and J4811 - all lots showing material code inconsistencies or temporal gaps with the Rev 3 changeover
D) Lot J4811 only - the maintenance log indicates old 6061 alloy was used on March 23 despite SAP showing 6063
rationale: This scenario tests temporal consistency across formal systems (SAP, ECN) and informal channels (Excel maintenance log). Answer A fails because it includes only J4801-J4805, missing the critical Lot J4811 problem. While J4801-J4805 were indeed produced before Rev 3 effectivity under Rev 2 governance and their SAP relabeling destroyed as-built traceability, J4811 has a separate material substitution issue that makes it equally suspect. Answer B fails because it sweeps in all 8 lots unnecessarily. Lots J4812-J4813 were produced March 25 onwards after the damaged 6063 alloy was replenished, and J4812 was specifically used for First Article Inspection verification — confirming correct 6063 material. The SAP material master creation timing (09:15 vs 10:00) is administrative setup, not evidence of material contamination across all lots. Answer D fails because it catches only J4811 while ignoring the equally problematic J4801-J4805 lots that were retroactively relabeled under a Rev 3 part number despite being physically produced under Rev 2 specifications (material: 6061-T6). The correct answer (C) identifies both problem groups: J4801-J4805 (traceability destroyed by SAP relabeling during cutover, confirmed by legacy material code format MAT-6061T6-LD) and J4811 (maintenance Excel reveals undocumented 6061 material substitution on March 23, contradicting SAP's 6063 coding). The critical informal signal — Jerry Santos's Excel entry about borrowing old 6061 stock — captured a plant-floor decision invisible to all formal systems.
